newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bank of Israel welcomes inflation goal.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Israel welcomes inflation goal.

text.p: Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel on Wednesday welcomed a new long-term official target of "Western"-level inflation, which he defined as about three percent a year.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Tuesday rejected a central bank demand for a specific multi-year inflation goal.
But Frenkel applauded the decision to achieve "Western" levels of inflation by the year 2001.

"For the first time the prime minister has decided he wants to see the inflation in Israel by the end of the decade or start of the coming decade at a 'Western' level, which today is about three percent," Frenkel said in an interivew with Israel Radio.
"I see yesterday's decision as most important because here it has been determined for the first time that the government is adopting a long-term strategy to lower inflation in Israel."
Netanyahu's government has set a 1997 inflation target of seven to 10 percent and promised to set a 1998 goal in the first half of next year, Treasury and central bank sources said.
The government had set an eight to 10 percent inflation target for 1996, but inflation is expected to exceed 10 percent.

"The decision regarding the inflation target for the coming year, which will be seven to 10 percent, is obviously an acceptable decision and it's important because it reflects progress in comparison with what there was this year," Frenkel said.
"It also reflects some sort of recognition that the struggle until now is succeeding."

Asked why, given the new targets and government promises of budget cuts, Frenkel was still resisting lowering interest rates, the Bank of Israel governor said: "Policy is not conducted based on declarations but achievements."
Frenkel also told the radio: "It's very important that there be a cut not only in the deficit of the government but in the expenditures of the government.
"We cannot raise taxes...the money must be left in the hands of the public and the economic decisions in the hands of the public," he added.
